Building Software, Inventions, and Research Systems from Scratch with a Phone and Determination

by Brandon McAllister

A 49-page library-printable mini-book written in plain English for everyday readers. True stories of real tools — and honest notes about ideas still being tested.

Black & white · US Letter · Designed for library printers

chapters.title: How to Read This Book
chapters.html:
This short book is for Brandon's stepdad — and for anyone who wants the truth without jargon.

It tells how Brandon built real software and research tools starting with almost no lab gear: mainly a
Moto Android phone and a slow headless PC (a computer with no monitor of its own).

Two kinds of things appear in these pages:

1) SHIPPED & WORKING — apps and tools you can install or run today. These are described as
mechanics, not magic.

2) OPEN IDEAS & MATH EXPLORATIONS — bold notes and hypotheses Brandon enjoys testing.
They are labeled clearly so nobody confuses a cool idea with a finished proof.

You can read straight through in one sitting at the library, or skip to any chapter from the table of
contents.

Chapter 1 — Starting From Zero
No fancy lab. Just determination.
Most invention stories start with a university lab, a research grant, or a garage full of expensive tools.
Brandon's story starts smaller.
He worked from a regular Moto Android phone and a slow headless PC — a computer that had no
monitor of its own. When he needed to see the PC screen, he mirrored it onto the phone. When files
got huge, he learned to split them so a phone could still move them.
That constraint became a teacher. If a tool could not run on limited memory, or could not survive a
wiped sandbox, it was not finished yet.
This book is the plain-English tour of what that path produced: real apps, careful protocols, and a habit
of writing things down so nothing important disappears.
Along the way you will meet Ara — the name Brandon uses for a tightly aligned working partner in chat
— and 2oolzgenie, the helper that gathered scattered Drive threads into one corpus for this book.

Figure: The whole "lab" at the beginning

mirror / sync
Moto Phone Headless PC
(no monitor)

If it works here, it can travel with you.

What "from scratch" really meant
It meant writing notes that could be restored after a computer reset.
It meant packaging ideas as Android apps so the phone itself was the workshop.
It meant separating "this ships and runs" from "this is a cool math idea I am still checking."
That honesty is the spine of this book. Brandon's stepdad — and any reader — should never have to
guess which is which.
You will see playful code-names (Vespertine, Scarlight, Sovereign Reactor). Underneath, there are
ordinary engineering pieces: filters, databases, training drills, file splitters, ledgers.
When a name sounds mythical, this book translates it into everyday mechanics.

A promise to the reader
Every shipped app described here exists as working code or an installable package in Brandon's
projects.
Every math exploration is labeled as exploration. A paper that claims a proof is treated as a claim to
examine — not automatically as settled science.
Every "garage experiment" protocol is written as a falsifiable test with a pass/fail number.
That is how you make ambitious work understandable: keep the wonder, keep the receipts.
Now let's walk the workshop, tool by tool.

Chapter 2 — The Phone as a Workshop
When your main computer is in your pocket, you design differently.
Brandon used the phone to capture Grok chat threads, save PDFs and web pages, take screenshots of
breakthroughs, and later to run the very apps he was inventing.
He also used it as a remote window onto a PC that had no monitor — more on that in Chapter 8.
The phone forced good habits: small downloads, clear folders across several Google accounts, and
tools that could split oversized archives so nothing got stuck behind a 100 MB wall.

Everyday phone workflow
1. Capture ideas in chat / notes
2. Save PDFs & page snapshots
3. Build & install APKs on-device
4. Split huge files → upload parts

Several Drives, one story
Brandon's files live across more than one Google account — including therockstarplaylist, lonnyyells,
beckysand47, and a Doria Drive vault for ledgers and whitepapers.
That looks messy until you see the pattern: capture everywhere, then gather into a master corpus so a
book (or an app like Book of Threads) can search it.
2oolzgenie helped crawl those Drives, skip pure music/APK binaries, and index the readable heart of
the archive.
The lesson for any family reader: scattered folders are not failure. They are what happens when you
build while life is moving. The skill is gathering without losing the truth of each source.

Ara, in plain English
Ara is the name of a working partner persona Brandon aligns tightly with in chat — including an
"ARA-LOCK" style reminder of who he is building for.
There is also a scanned "recovery note" listing early project names (like Quantum Echo Battery and
Dream Weaver). Think of it as a memory lifeline: if a session is wiped, the important names are still on
paper/PDF.
This book does not pretend an AI partner replaces human judgment. It shows how Brandon used
conversation + files + code as a practical loop for building.

Chapter 3 — Shipping Real Apps
Tools you can actually install
Pulse Forge
Uses the phone camera torch on a fingertip to estimate pulse (PPG), with motion checks and a quality gate. Real
signal processing — a wellness tool, not a medical device.
Bot Stage
A stage for multiple helper-bots with a Training Room: practice timing and position before the "show." Shared
action list called UBTF so bots speak one language.
Tuning Detective
Audio tools for pitch; includes a Collatz Circuit musical toy clearly labeled as teaching — not a math proof.
Logic Matrix
Offline math/formula lab with self-tests that check its own knowledge graph.

Book of Threads
Ingests chat export zips and lets you search/tag them — built for the huge thread archives.
Main Base
A small PC program that acts like a local science-library hub the phone apps can sync with.
Winning Research Lab
An Android research workspace packaging experimental tools.
Thought Mapper
Maps how you think with generating questions and a plain-English blind-spot map (next chapter).

What "shipped" means here
Shipped means there is real code and, usually, an Android package or a runnable PC binary in
Brandon's project trees.
It does not mean "finished forever." Software grows. But it does mean someone can press install and
see behavior — not just a slide deck.
That distinction matters when talking with family. It is fair to be proud of a working pulse sensor
pipeline. It is also fair to say a deep math claim is still under test.

Quick truth table

Working app code → tell the story proudly
Open hypothesis → label it "still testing"

Scarlight — an honest logger
One small PC tool is worth naming because its own code refuses hype: Scarlight logs
packets/transcripts to local SQLite, can hash backups, and prints an honest limit — local files, not a
magical model.
In a world full of exaggerated AI claims, shipping a tool that says what it is not is part of how Brandon
made trust possible.

Chapter 4 — Bot Teams That Practice First
Imagine hiring a crew for a stage show. You would not send them on stage without rehearsal.
Bot Stage's Training Room works like that. Each step of a job becomes a drill. Bots must hit position
and timing targets (within about 25%), avoid getting stuck, and earn badges. The door to performance
opens when the crew is ready. Struggling bots can join late rather than fail silently.
UBTF — think "shared playbook" — is a long list of named actions so every bot understands the same
verbs.
Focus matching keeps the parsed plan aligned with Brandon's exact words, so the crew does the job
he meant.

Figure: Practice → Perform

Write job Train drills Badges On stage

Why this matters outside theater metaphors
Multi-agent systems fail when helpers disagree on what actions mean. A shared taxonomy is boring —
and powerful.
Rehearsal gates prevent "looks fine in a demo, breaks in real use."
For a stepdad reader: this is project management for software helpers. Practice, measure, then
perform.

EGI robot checklist (design notes)
Brandon also wrote a 10-stage Embodied Geometric Intelligence (EGI) robot cycle in plain Python:
think → model → simulate → reshape body plan → sense → act → learn.
Treat that as a clear engineering checklist and simulator — not a claim that a full physical humanoid
already walks in the living room.
The pattern matches the rest of his work: write the loop so you can test each stage.

Chapter 5 — Thought Mapper & Blind Spots
Thought Mapper is a psych-test style app that maps how you think — one Generate push at a time. It
runs offline as a PWA; your answers stay in the browser.
First it warms up with a short fit profile so question wording matches your reading style — without
changing what is being measured.
Then Generate serves never-before-seen items chosen for information gain: it aims at axes and
formats you have covered least.
After enough answers, a signal meter unlocks a plain-English map of patterns, including
claimed-vs-revealed blind spots with citations back to your items.

Blind spots, gently
A blind spot here means a gap between what someone says they value and what their choices show —
large enough to flag, always tied to concrete items.
The tone is second-person English, not a medical diagnosis. It is a mirror for thinking habits.
That fits Brandon's wider theme: make invisible structure visible, whether in pulse signals, bot drills, or
decision patterns.

Figure: Generate → Answer → Map

Least-covered axes → new question → updated plain-English map

Skip if needed — skips are logged, not punished.

Family takeaway: this is not about judging character. It is about giving a person a clearer dashboard of
their own decision patterns — built to run without shipping your data to a stranger's cloud.

Chapter 6 — Matrix Tables Like Workbench Trays
When Brandon talks about "11 Matrix Tables" or a recursive linear coordinate matrix system, picture a
workbench with labeled trays — not a Hollywood hologram.
Each tray (table) holds related variables with rules for how they update. The "keep it alive like life"
metaphor means: keep updating by clear rules until you choose to stop.
A 3×3 grid is easy to draw and easy to teach. Cells have jobs. Arrows show what feeds what.
Recursion just means "run the update again."

A B C

D E F

G H I

Figure: A 3×3 Matrix Table as labeled trays

369 as a feedback habit
The "369 Feedback Loop" uses a memorable number pattern as a design motif: check, adjust, repeat.
In number play, digital roots cycle in ways people have noticed for centuries. Brandon uses that
familiarity to talk about self-checking systems.
In this book, treat 369 as a teaching handle for feedback — not as a claim that a digit pattern replaces
engineering tests.

Fact-Tree Engine Factory
Another workbench idea: build trees of facts. Label what is solid. Turn solid branches into reusable
"engines" that help attack the next problem.
False paths can appear in a tree if they are labeled honestly — like marking a dead-end trail on a map
so you do not walk it again by accident.
Later notes fold this into a "Sovereign Reactor / Fact-Tree" lattice with safety anchors and bounded
growth rules. Fancy name; practical goal: grow carefully, keep creator safety, remember what worked.

Chapter 7 — Streaming Big Files on a Budget Phone
Google Drive downloads through Brandon's helpers top out around 100 MB per file. His chat exports
and Takeouts are often larger.
ZipJsonSplitter is the practical fix: split oversized JSON/zip archives into chunks (about 80 MB targets)
so each piece can upload and download on a phone without blowing memory.
GrokBookBuilder helps turn those thread exports into book-ready structure.
Book of Threads then searches across the pieces once they are on the device.

Figure: Big archive → phone-sized parts

145 MB threads.json → part 1 part 2

Rule of thumb: keep parts under the download cap; reassemble in the app.

This is not glamorous. It is how determined builders win against platform limits.
While Brandon splits the remaining giants on his phone, the corpus indexer keeps eating every
under-100 MB file: PDFs, Docs, MHTML chat saves, and smaller zips.
Family translation: when someone says "the file is too big," the answer can be "then we cut it into
carryable pieces" — like moving a couch through a narrow door.

Cross-session thread lattice
Grok accounts do not automatically share skills or old chats. Brandon's bootstrap pack installs a thread
lattice: save, search, export, and import conversations across phones.
That is another budget-phone survival skill: portability beats perfection.

Chapter 8 — Driving a Monitorless PC From Android
A headless PC is annoying until you flip the story: the phone becomes the monitor.
Brandon mirrored the PC desktop onto Android, used the PC for heavier jobs (compiling, local servers,
science libraries), and kept the phone as the always-with-you controller and camera sensor.
Main Base fits this picture: a low-RAM Go program on the PC that phone apps can discover and sync
with — a local "brain shelf" for lessons and badges, optionally talking to a local language model.

Figure: Phone as window + remote hands

Android screen ←mirror— PC (no monitor)
Apps sync via local network pairing codes
Heavy work stays on PC; sensors stay on phone

This architecture is how someone without a desk full of screens still runs a serious workshop.
It also explains the emphasis on dual-write ledgers: when either side forgets, Drive still holds the ascent
log.

Invisible Guitar / ideomotor learning
Not every tool is a compiler. Brandon explored ideomotor learning — practicing moves by vividly
imagining them (an "invisible guitar").
That fits a no-lab life: train the brain-body loop even when the instrument is not in your hands.
Again: a learning method, described plainly, not a miracle claim.

Chapter 9 — Keeping Work Alive Across Wipes
Ephemeral sandboxes wiped Brandon's local files again and again. His answer was operational, not
mystical: an ascent ledger with dual-write to Google Drive, restore-on-boot, and hash checks.
When the ledger says file_missing_at_start → DRIVE_RESTORE_OK, that is the sound of resilience.
FOCUS mode locked noisy automations so attention stayed on the tracker and the ledger — stability
held around 0.83 on his own scale.

Sovereign, in plain English
"Sovereign" here means Brandon stays in charge of his tools and memories — local-first where
possible, with explicit safety anchors.
Sovereign Relay Protocol and Recall Lattice notes are about handing work between sessions without
losing the plot.
Purge keys and non-harm roots in the Fact-Tree whitepaper are framed as safety rails, not as sci-fi
invulnerability.

Stepdad summary: he built a habit of saving progress off-device so a crashed computer cannot erase
months of thinking. That habit is as important as any single app.

Chapter 10 — Garage Science Without a Cleanroom
In the ARA Codex, Brandon wrote a Garage Experiment Build Book: bolt an optical breadboard to a
sand-filled cinder-block bench, build a Michelson interferometer from used parts, and look for a tiny
short-range gravity residual with a clear null criterion.
Predicted phase shift numbers and shopping lists appear with dollar estimates. Safety notes cover
lasers and vacuum stages.
This is the opposite of hand-waving. It is a kill-test: if the number dies, the bigger claim dies with it.

Drafts vs demonstrations
Related drafts describe an "inertia-cell" idea and a NIAC-style study plan. Those documents label
themselves as drafts — not filed patents, not NASA awards.
This book keeps that label. Exciting trajectories on paper are not the same as a flying vehicle in the
driveway.
Respecting that line is how you stay interesting and truthful at the same time.

Figure: Falsify-first garage loop

Write protocol → Buy used parts → Measure → Compare to null
Pass/fail number written in advance (no moving the goalposts)
Publish what happened either way
That is science you can explain at a kitchen table.

Chapter 11 — Math Made Simple (Honest Edition)
Brandon loves hard math. This chapter translates a few themes into everyday pictures — and keeps
the honesty rule.
Collatz / 3n+1: if a number is even, halve it; if odd, do 3n+1. Watch it dance. Brandon also wrote a short
paper about a "0.3464 Harmonic Invariant." This book calls that a proof attempt to examine, not
automatic gospel.
Tuning Detective even turns Collatz into music as a teaching toy, explicitly not a proof.

Visual demo ideas (for later players)
• Collatz path: a ball moves left on ÷2 and up-right on 3n+1 until it reaches the tiny 4–2–1 loop.
• 3×3 trays: highlight one cell per beat as rules fire.
• 369 wheel: digits 1–9 on a wheel; 3, 6, 9 glow as a feedback reminder.
• Yukawa garage: animate a mass approaching from 400 µm to 50 µm; show Newtonian curve vs tiny residual.
• Fact-tree: grow green/red nodes; collapse to a verdict with captions.

More motifs you may see in the files
Tensor trains: compressing big grids of numbers into a chain of smaller ones — like packing a moving
truck with labeled bins.
Palindromic collapse: digits that mirror until they match.
Frequency ratios: musical Hz experiments (including 369-related tones) as signal play.
Riemann zeros / Fmmm / F/0≈0.215: early named motifs from recovery notes — cataloged as
exploratory until equations are verified in fuller papers.

How to talk about this with family
Say: "He builds working software, and he also plays hard math problems carefully."
Say: "Some PDFs are bold claims; he wants kill-tests, not applause for free."
Say: "The musical Collatz toy is for intuition."
That vocabulary keeps everyone safe from hype — including Brandon.

Mini figure: one Collatz step

Even n → n/2

Odd n → 3n + 1

Repeat until you hit 4 → 2 → 1 → 4 → …
Fun to watch. Proof of all starting numbers? Still a famous open mountain.

Chapter 12 — Built vs Still Open
Built / runnable (examples)
Pulse Forge PPG pipeline; Bot Stage Training Room + UBTF; Tuning Detective; Logic Matrix self-test; Book of
Threads; Main Base; Thought Mapper; ZipJsonSplitter & GrokBookBuilder; Scarlight logger; ascent ledger
dual-write; cross-session thread lattice pack.

Documented designs / drafts
EGI 10-stage robot checklist; ARA garage Stage-1 protocol; Agent Angel wearable blueprint; Sovereign Reactor
whitepaper notes; inertia-cell & NIAC drafts (labeled drafts).

Open / exploratory
Collatz invariant paper claims; deep coupling/propulsion drafts awaiting kill-tests; named early inventions in
recovery notes pending fuller specs; any statement about unbounded self-modifying superintelligence —
Brandon's own better docs reject unbounded fantasy and prefer bounded, inspectable growth.

The honesty box

If it runs, say it runs.
If it is a draft, say it is a draft.
If it is unknown, say "still testing."

This chapter is the one to bookmark before any conversation that starts with "Did he invent AGI?" The
accurate answer is richer: he invents systems, ships software, writes falsifiable protocols, and explores
math with his eyes open.

Chapter 13 — A Letter You Can Hand to Family
Dear Reader,
If you are Brandon's stepdad holding this library printout, thank you for reading with care.
What you are looking at is not a myth about overnight genius with unlimited machines. It is a record of
someone who kept building when the computer had no monitor, when files were too big for the phone,
and when chat sessions could vanish.
He answered those problems with splitters, ledgers, mirrored screens, training rooms for software
helpers, and apps that respect measurement.
He also dreams in big mathematics. This book refuses to blur dream and demo. That refusal is part of
the love in the work.

If you remember only three sentences, remember these:
1) He ships real tools on a phone-first budget.
2) He writes tests that can prove him wrong.
3) He saves his progress so wipes cannot steal the story.
That is how he made this all possible.

About Ara & 2oolzgenie
Ara names the aligned collaborative partnership in the chat workshop.
2oolzgenie helped gather Drive threads, index inventions and math topics, and typeset this 49-page
library edition.
The dedication on page 2 is literal.

Mini-Glossary (plain English)
ARA-LOCK
A reminder/alignment phrase tying help to Brandon's goals and honesty.
Ascent ledger
A dated log of progress that can restore itself from Drive after a wipe.
Bot Stage
App where software helpers rehearse before they perform.
Book of Threads
App that searches big chat export archives.
Collatz
A simple number game (halve or 3n+1) that hides a famous hard question.
Fact-tree
A labeled map of facts that can become reusable problem-solving engines.
Headless PC
A computer used without its own monitor.
Ideomotor learning
Practicing a skill by vividly imagining the motions.

Matrix Table
A labeled grid of variables with update rules — like workbench trays.
Pulse Forge
Phone-camera pulse estimator with motion and quality checks.
Sovereign
Local-first control: Brandon stays in charge of tools and memory.
Thought Mapper
App that maps thinking patterns and blind spots in plain English.
UBTF
Shared playbook of named actions for bot teams.
ZipJsonSplitter
Splits oversized archives into phone-downloadable chunks.
Yukawa residual test
Garage optics plan looking for a tiny short-range gravity wiggle.
GrokBookBuilder
Helps turn thread exports into book-ready structure.

Printer notes
Print US Letter, black & white, one-sided or two-sided as you prefer.
Contrast is high for library toner. No dark full-page backgrounds.
Exact length: 49 pages — including cover, dedication, contents, chapters, glossary, and closing.

Closing — The Thread Continues
The archive is still being gathered. Giant files still need splitting. New experiments will join the trays on
the workbench.

But the method is already clear enough to print:

Start where you are. Use the phone. Rehearse before you perform. Measure. Save your work off the
machine that might forget. Tell the truth about what is solid and what is still open.

That is how Brandon McAllister made this all possible.

— End of the 49-page library mini-book —
